Article Title: With Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff sitting next to him; Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to Wall Street worried about software companies: We are not here to …
Article Text:
With Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff next to him, Amodei emphasised that the company views the expansion of AI as a mutually beneficial, collaborative evolution across the technology sector.

What is ' SaaSpocalypse ' and how Wall Street reacted to it

Concerns in industry over data security

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has sought to reassure Wall Street investors, asserting that his frontier artificial intelligence (AI) lab has no intention of dismantling traditional enterprise software companies. Addressing long-standing investor concerns that generative AI tools will make traditional Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) business models obsolete, Amodei emphasised that the company views the expansion of AI as a mutually beneficial, collaborative evolution across the technology sector.“We're not interested in destroying anyone. We think of this as a very positive sum thing, right?," Amodei said, appearing alongside Salesforce Chief Executive Officer Marc Benioff on CNBC.Wall Street anxieties peaked in late January following Anthropic’s unveiling of plugins for Claude Cowork, an announcement that sparked widespread sell-offs dubbed the “SaaSpocalypse” and erased roughly $1 trillion in market value across the software industry in a single week.However, established software providers have mounted a strong recovery. For example, Salesforce recorded its second-best single trading day in corporate history last week, trailing only its historic growth surge during the COVID-19 pandemic.Ahead of its latest quarterly financial results, Salesforce revealed a deepened integration with the AI lab, branded internally as “Claudeforce.”Moreover, during the company's second-quarter earnings call, Benioff pushed back against market skeptics, noting that while analysts predicted seat contractions and customer departures, Salesforce logged year-over-year growth across Slack, Services and Agentforce Sales, while client attrition dropped to near-record lows.Amodei described the expanded tie-up as a classic synergistic combination where both organisations heavily utilise each other's technologies to deliver value that exceeds the sum of its individual parts.Prominent tech executives have voiced caution regarding frontier AI labs. Palantir CEO Alex Karp recently warned enterprises to strictly protect their proprietary data, competitive edge and intellectual property when interacting with AI providers.Karp cautioned earlier this month against adopting technologies that could compromise enterprise autonomy, profitability, and domestic economic strength.
Article Summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei sought to reassure Wall Street investors, asserting that his frontier artificial intelligence (AI) lab has no intention of dismantling traditional enterprise software companies. Wall Street anxieties peaked in late January following Anthropic’s unveiling of plugins for Claude Cowork, an announcement that sparked widespread sell-offs dubbed the “SaaSpocalypse”

Article Title: As death toll in heatwave-hit Europe crosses 30,000; scientists suggest companies to push this almost 20-year old portable gadget in their offices
Article Text:
Representative image

What the study found

How the experiment worked

Why a small breeze can cool the whole body

Why offices without reliable AC are the best candidates

As the death toll from Europe’s ongoing heatwave climbs past 30,000, scientists are urging companies to consider unconventional cooling solutions for their offices. Among them: wearable neck fans, a nearly 20-year-old gadget which has long struggled to gain mainstream acceptance due to its ‘dork factor’. According to a report by Popular Science, a recent study in the journal E3S Web of Conferences found that portable neck and face fans performed nearly as well as bladeless desk fans in keeping office workers cool. While not as powerful as traditional bladed fans, they offered key advantages: lower energy use, less disruption to coworkers, and targeted cooling for thermosensitive areas like the neck and face.In controlled testing, portable neck and face fans performed roughly as well as bladeless desk fans at keeping office workers comfortable. They fell short of matching traditional bladed desk fans in raw cooling power, but came with two practical advantages: they don't blow large gusts of air toward nearby coworkers who might prefer a warmer setting, and they use considerably less energy than either desktop alternative.Mohamed Ouf, an engineering professor at Concordia University in Canada and co-author of the study, said in a statement that these fans offer a way to keep a centralized HVAC system running while using less energy overall — a detail that matters directly to employers looking to cut cooling costs.Researchers tested four devices — a neck fan, a face fan, a bladed desktop fan, and a bladeless desk fan — each evaluated at both low and high speed settings. To avoid the subjectivity of asking human subjects how comfortable they felt, the team removed humans from the experiment entirely. Instead, they directed airflow from each device toward a life-sized, 23-segment thermal manikin modeled after an average Scandinavian man. The manikin was outfitted with sensors that continuously track skin temperature, heat loss, and predicted thermal comfort across different regions of the body, allowing researchers to measure precisely how quickly its surface cooled and returned to a comfortable baseline.The manikin was dressed in standard summer office attire — a short-sleeve shirt, pants, and sneakers — and placed in a test room designed to mimic a typical office cubicle, with the thermostat set to 77 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature warm enough to cause noticeable discomfort without being extreme.The neck fan performed nearly as well as the bladeless desk fan overall. Despite producing a much smaller, more localized breeze than a desktop fan, the wearable device delivered whole-body comfort in the data, a result researchers attribute to how thermosensitive the neck and face are. That region accounts for only about 5.5% of a person's total body surface area, but plays an outsized role in overall temperature regulation and perceived comfort.Neither wearable device could match the sheer output of a traditional bladed desk fan, but both offered meaningful trade-offs: they take up far less desk space, use less energy, and direct airflow only at the wearer — avoiding the common office annoyance of a desk fan blasting air into a neighbouring cubicle.The findings may seem irrelevant to workers in buildings with dependable central air conditioning running by default, but researchers note that this assumption doesn't hold everywhere. Many offices outside the United States still don't rely on air conditioning at all. Even in buildings that do, the shift to hybrid work is changing incentives — with fewer employees occupying large office floors on any given day, cost-conscious building owners may see less value in fully cooling entire spaces. Faced with that math, some employers may opt to raise the thermostat and instead point employees toward a personal wearable fan as a cheaper alternative to full building-wide cooling.
Article Summary: portable neck and face fans performed nearly as well as bladeless desk fans in keeping office workers cool. While not as powerful as traditional bladed fans, they offered key advantages: lower energy use, less disruption to coworkers, and targeted cooling for thermosensitive areas like the neck.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu warns against a world driven entirely by profit: ‘Do we want …’
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Ve​mbu

Sridhar Vembu says profit should support society's foundations

Sridhar Vembu: Technology should be a means, not the final goal

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has raised questions about whether every part of human life should be driven by profit, arguing that modern economic thinking risks creating a “dystopian world” when activities such as farming, teaching and healthcare are viewed mainly through a commercial lens. In a post shared on X (formerly Twitter), Sridhar Vembu asked whether society wants its farmers, teachers, doctors and priests to become profit-driven. “Do we want our farmers, teachers, doctors and priests to be profit-driven?,” he wrote. Vembu argued that modern finance and economic theory encourages almost all human activity to focus on profit, while overlooking the deeper social, cultural and spiritual foundations on which markets themselves depend.“Modern finance and economic theory encourages essentially all human activity to be profit-driven. This leads to a dystopian world,” he wrote.Sridhar Vembu said the modern idea of the market is built on a wider “bedrock” of human civilisation, spirituality and culture that is not itself driven by market forces. According to him, some schools of economic thought either ignore this foundation or argue that economic forces shape everything else.He then raised a broader question about who should support these parts of society.“The ones who are in the ‘market’, companies like us,” Vembu wrote, suggesting that businesses have a role beyond generating financial returns.Vembu went further, arguing that the purpose of profit should be to help sustain what he described as society's basic foundations. He grouped these under four ideas: nature, nurture, culture and scripture, linking them to food, education, entertainment and spiritual life.The Zoho founder also shared his view on the role of technology, saying it should serve a larger purpose rather than become an end in itself.“I look at technology as the means to an end, not an end itself,” Vembu wrote.
Article Summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says profit should support society's foundations. He argues that modern economic thinking risks creating a ‘dystopian world’ He asks whether society wants its farmers, teachers, doctors and priests to be profit- driven. Vem Bu also says technology should be a means, not the final goal.

Article Title: How a Chinese company is using Blue Light to fight mosquitoes, claims 30 kills per second: Scans the area, locks on in 3 milliseconds and...
Article Text:
Blue laser fires, mosquito drops: Photon Matrix claims 30 kills a second

How the Photon Matrix laser mosquito killer finds a 2mm target in the dark

The blue laser mosquito zapper's safety case has no independent testing behind it

The mosquito laser is a 20-year-old idea that finally shipped

Mosquitoes kill roughly 700,000 people a year, which makes them the deadliest animal on the planet by a wide margin. Our defences have not changed much in a century: nets, coils, sprays, and a rolled-up newspaper. A startup in Changzhou, in eastern China, thinks the next step is a laser turret that sits on your patio and shoots the insects out of the air.Photon Matrix has opened preorders for its blue laser mosquito air defense system at $1,088, roughly Rs 95,000, after starting mass production in August. The company says the device locks onto a mosquito in three milliseconds and can take down up to 30 of them a second, in complete darkness, without chemicals and without noise. Those are the company's own numbers, and nobody outside the company has verified them yet.The unit scans a flat fan of light across the space in front of it and continuously measures how far away the background is. When something small crosses that plane, the distance reading changes. The system then checks the size, and if it matches a mosquito, between 2mm and 20mm moving slower than a metre per second, an internal galvo mirror points the laser down the same optical path the LiDAR just used and burns the wings.Coverage is a six-metre radius across a 90-degree arc, and a rotating base spins the device for something closer to full coverage. A companion app logs kills, plots a mosquito heat map, sets on-off schedules and, for reasons known only to the marketing team, ranks you on a global leaderboard.The obvious question about a laser strong enough to disable an insect is what happens when it misses. Photon Matrix's answer is a background check: the laser fires only when it detects a solid surface within range, and shuts off when it cannot find one. The company says the system has cleared certifications covering people, pets and birds, and that it ignores butterflies and other larger insects. It has also promised to publish more testing and safety data. Until an independent reviewer gets a unit on a table, buyers are taking that on trust, and the comment sections under every video of this thing are full of people asking about eyes.There are two versions. The outdoor blue laser model at $1,088 flashes visibly each time it fires. The indoor infrared model, at $988 or about Rs 87,000, uses a 976nm invisible beam pitched at bedrooms and hotel rooms. Both come with a rotating base, a 12-month warranty and a 20,000mAh power bank good for around four hours off mains. Delivery is quoted at roughly 120 days.The project raised $2.7 million on Indiegogo against a $20,000 target, with over 4,000 backers paying about $630 each, then slipped repeatedly on sensor calibration and safety approvals. The concept itself dates to 2006, when an astrophysicist who worked on Reagan-era missile defence pitched it at a brainstorming session. A prototype turret with a 50-metre range was demonstrated in 2010 and never found a buyer.So the century-old arsenal gets a new entry, and it works out to about a thousand dollars for the privilege of watching mosquitoes fall.
Article Summary: Photon Matrix claims its laser can take down 30 mosquitoes a second. It uses a LiDAR to measure distance and size of the target. The laser fires only when it detects a solid surface within range, and shuts off when it cannot find one.

Article Title: After 101-years, this California business is shutting down on August 31; owner says in an emotional note: Decision comes with ...
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation only

Why the 101 year shop is shutting down

What the note on shutting down says

Hank & Frank Bicycles Announces Retirement After 101 Years of Community Service

After more than a century of serving Bay Area riders, families, and adventurers, Hank & Frank Bicycles will officially retire and close its doors on August 31, 2026. This decision comes with full hearts, deep gratitude, and an enduring love for the community that has carried us for generations.

A Legacy Built on Trust

Founded in 1925, Hank & Frank has been a rare constant in a changing world—a 101-years legacy stewarded by only two families.

When Dale Dryer took over the business from Hank 57 years ago, he carried forward a tradition of craftsmanship, honesty, and neighborly care. Today, as we prepare to close this chapter, we reflect with gratitude on the generations of customers, employees, friends, and families who made this shop far more than a place to buy or service a bicycle.

Why This Shop Has Always Mattered

Our “why” has always been simple: to help people experience the freedom, confidence, connection, and joy that a bicycle can bring.

Whether it was a child’s first ride, a family’s weekend adventure, a commuter’s daily route, or a lifelong cyclist’s next great bike, we have believed that every rider deserves care, respect, and guidance they can trust.

We have had the privilege of watching children grow up on our bikes—then return years later to buy bikes for their own children. We have seen families ride through milestones, seasons, and lifetimes with us.

From our original home on East 14th Street in Oakland, through several locations over the decades, to our final and beloved home in the City of Lafayette for the past 52 years, every community we have served has shaped who we are.

With Deep Gratitude

To all of you—our riders, neighbors, friends, and extended family—thank you. Thank you for your trust, your stories, your friendly smiles, your loyalty, and your belief in what a local bike shop can mean to a community.

You invited us into your lives at birthdays, graduations, weekend rides, first commutes, race days, repairs, upgrades, and ordinary moments that became lasting memories.

Your support allowed us to do what we loved for more than a century: serve people well, stand behind our work, and help keep generations of riders rolling safely, happily, and confidently. That is a gift we will never take for granted.

Looking Ahead

As we look ahead, we also look forward to wishing Frank a joyful and well-earned next chapter.

At the same time, we are actively seeking the right person to carry on this extraordinary legacy, and we will keep our community informed as that search continues.

Between now and August 31, 2026, we invite you to stop by and be part of this final season with us:

* Pick out your next quality bicycle.

* Schedule service with our exceptional mechanics.

* Share a memory, a story, or a simple hello.

* Let us thank you in person for being part of our journey.

It has been our honor to help keep you moving for so many years. More than anything, we hope you know how deeply grateful we are—for every mile shared, every relationship built, and every moment of trust you placed in us.

With sincere gratitude,

The Hank & Frank Team

Hank & Frank Bicycles

After more than 101 years in business, a Bay Area institution is closing up shop. The century-old fixture of the Bay Area cycling community will permanently close its doors at the end of the month, marking the end of an era for one of the region's oldest bike retailers. Hank & Frank Bicycles, which first opened in 1925, announced that its final day of business will be August 31.The shop began operations on East 14th Street in Oakland before relocating several times, eventually establishing its permanent home in Lafayette, where it has operated for the past 52 years. The business changed hands 57 years ago when Dale Dryer took over from original founder Hank. His son, Frank Dryer, grew up sweeping the floors and assembling tricycles before purchasing the Lafayette storefront from his father in 1991.Unlike many recent legacy business closures driven by online competition or rising operational costs, the shutdown comes as the building changes hands. The property’s new owners plan to convert the space into a dance studio, prompting the younger Dryer to choose retirement rather than relocate. Dryer noted that while he is saddened to leave the community, the timing felt right, particularly without a successor to carry on the family trade.Customer loyalty remained steady throughout the decades, bolstered by a longstanding promise of free lifetime tune-ups with every bicycle purchase. To honor that commitment after the storefront closes, Dryer has arranged for a neighboring independent shop in Walnut Creek to take over the lifetime service perk for existing patrons.Patrons and longtime cyclists are visiting the Lafayette location in its final days to purchase bikes, schedule tune-ups, and share farewell notes with the staff before the shop closes its doors for good on August 31.
Article Summary: Hank & Frank Bicycles, which first opened in 1925, announced that its final day of business will August 31. The shop began operations on East 14th Street in Oakland before relocating several times. The business changed hands 57 years ago when Dale Dryer took over from original founder Hank Dryer.

Article Title: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman joins Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai in their Space data center plans; says: Let’s take our data centers to ...
Article Text:
​NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman joins Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai in their Space data center plans

A political liability on the ground

Not the first time Jared Isaacman has floated the idea

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has joined Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai in support of relocating data centers to Earth’s orbit. Along with the CEOs of SpaceX and Google, Isaacman is also pushing this idea to sidestep growing public anger over the facilities' environmental and economic toll in American communities. In an interview with Nexstar DC's Vinay Simot, Isaacman said: "Let's take our data centers, put them in Earth orbit, take advantage of that free fusion reactor that's out there for us and use that to ensure we do win the … space race for sure, but the AI race, too,"In January, at the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, Elon Musk said that "the lowest-cost place to put AI will be in space, and that will be true within two years, maybe three at the latest," while Google CEO Sundar Pichai has said Alphabet is exploring "moonshot" concepts for data centers in space later this decade under an internal effort known as Project Suncatcher.Isaacman added that the move would "have immense benefits," as companies could leverage solar energy, which is the "free fusion reactor", to power data centers without straining terrestrial electric grids.Data centers, which fuel the growing AI industry, have quickly lost favour with the public with many saying their presence raises prices in communities and carries negative environmental impacts. Amid this pushback, US politicians are hastily trying to distance themselves from the facilities.Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, signed an order last week requiring that data center developers cover electricity costs and gain local backing for projects. Shapiro had previously boasted about these facilities' investments in his state.This is not the first time the NASA administrator has proposed the idea of sending data centers into space. In an early August appearance on the New York Post's "Pod Force One" podcast, Isaacman called the proposal a "fantastic" solution to the public's complaints."Elon [Musk] and others in the industry are like, 'Let's take the data centers that no one likes in your backyard — it seems like there's a lot of consensus on that — and put them into space where they won't bother anyone'," Isaacman said during the earlier podcast.He added that the space data centers would need solar panels "the size of several football fields.”
Article Summary: Jared Isaacman has joined Elon Musk and Sundar Pichai in support of relocating data centers to Earth’s orbit. Isaacman is also pushing this idea to sidestep growing public anger over the facilities' environmental and economic toll in American communities.

Article Title: Apple may launch AI-powered smart glasses in 202: Here’s what to expect
Article Text:
Apple smart glasses may use cameras to understand the real world

Apple smart glasses may use cameras to understand the real world

No display, but built-in speakers for music and calls

Health features may have to wait

Apple could make its entry into the smart glasses market as early as next year, with a product focused on artificial intelligence rather than augmented reality. According to reports, the company's first smart glasses are expected to combine cameras, Siri and built-in speakers to help users interact with the world around them, according to reports. Unlike AR glasses, they are not expected to have a display. Instead, users may be able to ask Siri questions about what they are seeing, translate signs and get information about their surroundings. Apple is also reportedly testing different designs as it prepares for a new category of AI-powered wearable devices.The reported glasses could use cameras and Apple's Visual Intelligence technology to help Siri understand what is around the wearer. This could allow users to ask questions about objects and places and receive relevant information.The glasses may also be able to translate text and signage. Another feature reportedly being considered would allow users to ask Siri to save an image of something and remind them about it later. However, the first-generation device may not work like a regular camera. Apple could reportedly limit the ability to take photos and videos, as privacy concerns around camera-equipped smart glasses continue to grow.Apple's first smart glasses are expected to be AI glasses rather than AR glasses. This means the device is not expected to place digital images or information directly in front of the user's eyes.Instead, the glasses could rely on voice commands, cameras and built-in speakers. The speakers could be used for music and other audio, potentially allowing the device to double as a pair of open-ear headphones.Apple is said to be developing the glasses in-house and is reportedly testing several designs. These include larger and slimmer rectangular frames, as well as oval and circular options. The frames could be made from acetate, a material considered more durable and premium than regular plastic. Reported colour options include black, ocean blue and light brown.Apple is reportedly also exploring health features for future versions of the smart glasses. These could include heart-rate monitoring and software tools designed to support fitness and wellness.But such features are not expected in the first version. For the initial model, Apple's focus appears to be on putting AI and Siri into a wearable device that could help users access information without having to constantly look at their phones.
Article Summary: Apple's first smart glasses are expected to be AI glasses rather than AR glasses. This means the device is not expected to place digital images or information directly in front of the user's eyes. Instead, the glasses could rely on voice commands, cameras and built-in speakers. Apple is said to be developing the glasses in-house and is reportedly testing several designs.

Article Title: Operation Bluebird startup launches Twitter.now, says it is not linked to Elon Musk's X
Article Text:
Operation Bluebird launches Twitter.now (AI-edited image)

A startup sees an opportunity after Twitter became X

A judge's comments gave the startup confidence to launch

Here’s what Operation Bluebird co-founder wrote on LinkedIn

The name Twitter has returned to the internet. A Virginia-based startup called Operation Bluebird has launched a new social media platform, Twitter.now, claiming that the Twitter name and some of its well-known intellectual property were abandoned after Elon Musk renamed Twitter to X. The launch comes despite an ongoing legal fight with X Corporation, which has challenged the startup's attempt to use the old Twitter identity. Operation Bluebird says its platform is not connected to X and is building a different kind of online public square, with automated fact-checking and more control for users over what they see.When Elon Musk acquired Twitter in 2022, he eventually renamed the platform X and replaced the familiar blue bird branding. Operation Bluebird believes that decision created an opportunity to reclaim the Twitter name.The startup's co-founder Stephen Coates, who previously served as general counsel at Twitter before Musk's takeover, said the company had waited for months before launching but did not want to delay further.Operation Bluebird's legal argument is that X Corporation abandoned its rights to trademarks linked to Twitter, including the word "Twitter," "tweet" and the bird logo. X Corporation, however, sued Operation Bluebird last year and sought to stop the new platform from launching.The legal dispute is still ongoing, and a final decision has not been issued.Legal dispute between Elon Musk’s X and Operation Bluebird continues.During an April 2026 hearing, US District Court Judge Colm Connolly gave a tentative ruling suggesting that X appeared to have given up its intellectual property claims over the word "tweet" and the Twitter bird logo. The judge also raised the possibility that rights to the word "Twitter" may have been abandoned.However, the judge has not yet issued a written order.The move could now intensify the legal battle. Trademark attorney Josh Gerben told Ars Technica that Operation Bluebird may have a workable legal argument, but said the case was far from straightforward and that X could respond strongly now that the platform has launched.In a LinkedIn post, Coates wrote:"Today, Operation Bluebird launched Twitter.now.When X Corp. retired the Twitter brand, we saw an opportunity to build something new: a public square organized around trust, transparency, and user choice.Twitter.now is not an attempt to recreate the old platform. We are building a different service, with trust signals that provide context for what users see and tools that allow people—not an opaque algorithm—to decide how much credibility and noise reach their feeds. Our governing principle is simple: freedom of speech, not freedom of reach.Twitter is a reclaimed brand. We are not X and are not affiliated with X Corp.Early access is now open. Founding members can help us build and test the platform, get first shot at the handle of their choice, and claim their place in its history—including Founder number #00001.The public square is open again, and definitely not affiliated with X in any way. Whatsoever.Get over your X. The bird is back."
Article Summary: Virginia-based startup Operation Bluebird has launched a new social media platform, Twitter.now. The launch comes despite an ongoing legal fight with X Corporation, which has challenged the startup's attempt to use the old Twitter identity. The legal dispute is still ongoing, and a final decision has not been issued.

Article Title: Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi warns: Never in the 35 years has there ever been a time when all things are screaming to tell you ...
Article Text:
Mark Zandi said he couldn't pinpoint exactly when a crisis might hit

The debt-to-GDP warning sign

National debt tops $40 trillion

Bond market turmoil intensifies

Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi has issued one of his starkest warnings yet, saying the US may be ‘sleepwalking’ into an economic crises. According a report by Moneywise, speaking on the Sonia and Simon podcast Zandi said, “Never in the 35 years has there ever been a time when all of the measures are screaming, you know, we got a problem”. He also cautioned that the preconditions for a reckoning are falling into place, even if the timing remains uncertain. Zandi pointed to America’s debt-to-GDP ratio crossing 100% in April, a level not seen since the aftermath of World War II. He highlighted the government’s $2 trillion annual budget deficit, which becomes harder to manage as interest rates rise. The cumulative national debt has now surpassed $40 trillion, with investors increasingly skeptical of US fiscal policy.Speaking on a recent episode of the Sonia and Simon podcast with hosts Sonia Jahshan and Simon Baggs, Zandi said he couldn't pinpoint exactly when a crisis might hit, but stressed that the underlying preconditions for one are already falling into place — and that he doesn't think the public fully appreciates how serious that is.Zandi went further, arguing that he believes it's essentially unavoidable that the U.S.will need some kind of external shock to force real fiscal change. He said he doesn't believe the American political system, or the public, is capable of making the difficult changes needed to address the country's long-term fiscal problems without being pushed into it by a crisis triggered by rising interest rates.Zandi pointed first to America's debt-to-GDP ratio, which crossed the 100% threshold at the end of April. That ratio measures the size of government debt relative to the overall economy, and offers insight into the federal government's long-term ability to repay what it owes. The U.S. hasn't reached triple-digit debt-to-GDP territory since the years immediately following World War II, when the ratio briefly peaked at 106%.Zandi also flagged the sheer size of the government's current $2 trillion annual budget deficit, noting that a deficit of that scale becomes even harder to manage as interest rates climb — which is exactly what's happening now, driven in part by investors selling off Treasury bonds to protect their portfolios against risks tied to the Iran war and the country's swelling debt load.The cumulative U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time last week, with little indication that its upward climb is slowing. Zandi said the country is issuing large amounts of new debt even as its fiscal position continues to erode, and warned that combining that trend with growing skepticism among global investors — skepticism he tied directly to policy decisions made over the past couple of years — creates the conditions for significantly higher interest rates ahead.The yield on 30-year Treasury bonds stood at 5.17% on August 25, hovering near multi-year highs. Earlier this month, it briefly topped 5.3%, its highest level since 2007. Bond yields matter well beyond Wall Street: they determine what investors earn for holding government debt, but they also directly influence borrowing costs for everyday consumers, including mortgage and auto loan rates, as well as how much the federal government itself pays in interest on the national debt.In response to the sell-off, the Treasury Department is set to begin buying back more of its own bonds starting in early September, an effort aimed at artificially suppressing interest rates.
Article Summary: Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi has issued one of his starkest warnings yet, saying the US may be ‘sleepwalking’ into an economic crises. Zandi said he couldn't pinpoint exactly when a crisis might hit, but stressed that the underlying preconditions for one are already falling into place. The cumulative U.S. national debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time last week.

Article Title: Apple 'Surprise and Shine' event on September 9: Foldable iPhone Ultra, iPhone 18 Pro and everything else to expect
Article Text:
The foldable iPhone is the biggest launch expected on the day

The iPhone 18 Pro upgrade sounds modest, the price rise may not be

Watches, AirPods and new home devices make up the rest of the list

Siri AI is the software behind most of these new devices

Apple has confirmed September 9 for its annual iPhone launch, and the invite sent out on Wednesday uses the tagline "Surprise and shine." The keynote starts at 10am Pacific, which is 10.30pm IST, and will stream from the Steve Jobs Theater at Apple Park via Apple's site, YouTube and the Apple TV app.Two things separate this from the usual September routine. It is the first Apple event with John Ternus running the company, since Tim Cook hands over the CEO title on September 1 and becomes executive chairman. The rumoured product list is also unusually long. Apple pushed the new Mac mini and Mac Studio out in late August, a slot it has used only once in the past decade, and several reports read that as an attempt to free up space on stage.The device drawing the most attention is Apple's first foldable, which most reports expect to be called iPhone Ultra. Leaks point to a 7.8-inch inner display that opens like a book and a roughly 5.3-inch cover screen, with the A20 Pro chip and 12GB of memory.Rumours suggest two 48MP rear cameras and no telephoto lens, which would be an odd omission at this price. There are also claims that authentication falls back to Touch ID rather than Face ID.Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, who says he has spoken to people who have used the phone, reports that the hinge and the way it fits in a pocket both impressed them, and that it works well as a camera viewfinder. He expects pricing to start above $2,000, roughly Rs 1.8 lakh before Indian duties, so the local figure would likely be higher.The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max are widely tipped as a spec-bump year. Reports point to a 2nm A20 Pro with packaging changes meant to help thermals, Apple's own C2 modem, a slightly larger camera bump and a dark cherry finish. A variable-aperture rear camera is rumoured to be a Pro Max exclusive, and under-display Face ID has been floated without much backing.Pricing is the bigger question. With memory costs climbing, Samsung and Google have each raised phone prices by about $100, and Gurman expects Apple to follow, which would put the iPhone 18 Pro near $1,199. Other estimates run steeper.The standard iPhone 18, the iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air are not expected in September, with reports pointing to 2027.Apple Watch Series 12 is expected to be a light update, with talk of a health sensor tied to a fluoroelastomer band, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 may get a redesign. AirPods 5 look likely, in ANC and non-ANC versions. The camera-equipped AirPods that leaked in a macOS Tahoe release candidate are still reported as a 2027 product.The home devices are the bigger unknown. Reports mention a refreshed Apple TV 4K, a new HomePod mini and a home hub with a seven-inch screen. Gurman reports Apple is reworking the accessory sections in its retail stores, which he takes as a sign of more than routine updates. An OLED iPad mini remains a wildcard.Most of the home hardware has reportedly been waiting on the Siri overhaul Apple previewed at WWDC in June. That keynote was structured differently from the usual run through each operating system in turn, with Apple instead laying out a cross-platform pitch built around Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.The version demoed uses large language model technology to let the assistant act inside apps such as Messages and Calendar rather than only answering questions. It is the feature Apple has been promising and delaying since 2024.Siri AI is expected alongside iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27 Tahoe, watchOS 27 and tvOS 27, reportedly in the back half of September and initially as a waitlisted beta. That timing matters for the hardware. A refreshed Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini would need newer chips to support it, which is one explanation for why those updates have taken so long, and a home hub with a screen makes little sense without an assistant that can act on requests.
Article Summary: Apple will launch the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max on September 9. The foldable phone is expected to start at around $2,000. Apple Watch Series 12 and AirPods are expected to be light updates. Siri AI is expected alongside iOS 27, iPadOS 27, watchOS 27 and tvOS 27.

Article Title: Bill Gates, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang does not agree with you; says: I love Bill, but he is wrong as ...
Article Text:
Jensen Huang has previously suggested that skilled, blue-collar workers stand to gain significantly from the AI boom

Jensen Huang says he is open to some taxes, just not this one

A bid for reindustrialisation

Jensen Huang has pushed back on a proposal from Bill Gates to tax robots and AI tokens. The Nvidia CEO has argued that his own approach to sharing the wealth generated by the AI boom would look different from what the Microsoft co-founder has suggested. In an interview with Fox Business's The Claman Countdown, Huang said: "I love the heck out of Bill … but I don't see what he sees. I see something very, very different. And so my remedies will be a little different."This comes after Gates published an essay this week, titled "The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical." In it, Gates wrote: "Right now, if you're an employer and you hire someone, you pay payroll taxes on their earnings. But if you buy a robot, you can usually write it off right away as a business expense. The tax system nudges you toward replacing people with machines."Gates argued that this imbalance in the tax code could accelerate the pace at which companies replace workers with machines. This isn't Gates' first attempt to float the robot tax idea; he originally raised the concept in 2017, when economists broadly dismissed it as essentially a tax on productivity gains.Gates has suggested that governments will need the funds, reasoning that if AI takes over human jobs, state revenues from income tax will drop. "A tax would slow the rush away from human labour a little and raise money for retraining and a stronger safety net," Gates explained."I'm in favour of taxes. And I think that … for anybody who is productive, it's a great way for us to contribute back to society and the economy. But the fact of the matter is, there are probably lots of different ways to approach this,” Huang added.Huang's perspective is more positive. He said that while "of course" the nature of jobs would change, as it already has. "I believe … that this will be a net job creator. However, there are going to be many jobs will be disrupted, so we have to be sensible about that. We have to be sensitive about that and be supportive of that,” he added.While Gates suggests that companies could be incentivised to replace humans with robots because of existing fiscal policy, Huang says the historical precedent disagrees: "When companies are more productive, they don't lay off people, they hire more people. The reason for that is because companies have ambitions … and I would say the vast majority of the world's companies … have ambitions for growth. When they're more productive, when they're more profitable, [it] allows us to invest more and go after more growth. Nonetheless, overall, this is going to be a net job creator at a scale that we have never seen."Huang has previously suggested that skilled, blue-collar workers stand to gain significantly from the AI boom. Trades like plumbers and electricians, Huang has said, will be in high demand as data centers are built across the globe.Speaking this week, the 63-year-old tech titan suggested that the new economic era would be one of reindustrialisation.He explained: "We have lots and lots of white-collar workers, but we're also going to have a lot of skilled labour. And having a large population of skilled labour and people who build things and make things with their hands is tremendous for the United States. We want to reindustrialise the United States. We want to create more jobs. And all of that's going to happen right now as we speak with AI."
Article Summary: Jensen Huang has pushed back on a proposal from Bill Gates to tax robots and AI tokens. The Nvidia CEO has argued that his own approach to sharing the wealth generated by the AI boom would look different from what the Microsoft co-founder has suggested. This comes after Gates published an essay this week titled "The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical"

Article Title: Google Messages gets customisation setting: How to use it

Here’s what OpenAI said on cutting off deal with Cursor

Elon Musk has responded after OpenAI said it is ending its partnership with Cursor, a coding tool recently acquired by Musk's SpaceX. The move ends a partnership that had been in place for around three years and adds a new chapter to the long-running dispute between Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. In an X (formerly Twitter) post, Musk appeared unfazed by the decision, saying he “couldn’t care less” and launching a fresh attack on Altman and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, calling them untrustworthy. “I couldn’t care less. Scam Altman and Greg Stockman are utterly untrustworthy assholes who stole an open source nonprofit,” Musk wrote in the post.Cursor was founded in 2022. It was recently acquired by Elon Musk’s space company SpaceX. Musk had sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman for "stealing a charity" by betraying the company's ​original nonprofit mission.“To work with a large partner like SpaceX, we typically rely on custom contracts to ensure compliance with our terms of service and that the integration provides for safety at scale. After Musk acquired Twitter, now part of SpaceX, the company broke⁠(opens in a new window) the terms of our contract (alongside many others).Under oath earlier this year, Musk admitted⁠(opens in a new window) that xAI, now also part of SpaceX, had violated OpenAI’s terms of service (terms which are similar to xAI’s own),” OpenAI said in an announcement.Reacting to the OpenAI announcement, Michael Truell, a co-founder of Cursor and now an executive at SpaceX shared an X post where he reiterated that Cursor was one of the very first users of OpenAI and that the space company is “speaking with the OpenAI team to resolve this”.“We’re sorry to see that OpenAI put out a note saying they plan to block Cursor users from accessing OpenAI models in three months,” Truell wrote in the post adding “OpenAI models serve about 5% of Cursor user traffic, and we’re speaking with the OpenAI team to resolve this”.“Cursor was one of the very first users of OpenAI, we’ve worked closely with their team for years, and we’ve trusted their platform to be neutral infrastructure for our business.”"Today, we notified SpaceX that we intend to wind down our contract providing OpenAI models to Cursor, with a proposed shutoff date of November 12, 2026. To maximize the time that developers can retain access to our models through Cursor, we are giving the maximum notice provided by our contract. This decision was incredibly tough, as we care deeply about our models being broadly available for developers. We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts.To work with a large partner like SpaceX, we typically rely on custom contracts to ensure compliance with our terms of service and that the integration provides for safety at scale. After Musk acquired Twitter, now part of SpaceX, the company broke⁠(opens in a new window) the terms of our contract (alongside many others). Under oath earlier this year, Musk admitted⁠(opens in a new window) that xAI, now also part of SpaceX, had violated OpenAI’s terms of service (terms which are similar to xAI’s own).Our custom agreement with Cursor gives us a limited time window to cancel it after a change of control. As AI capabilities advance, we also have a new level of accountability to ensure our upcoming model, Astra, is being used in accordance with our terms. Given all of this, we’ve decided to hold the contract cancellation to the latest date we can while not providing future models to Cursor.We’ve worked with Cursor for nearly four years and have enormous respect for their team, their product, and what they’ve built for the developer community. Article Title: Chinese company that Apple made a 'special request' to the US government for has sued Pentagon
Article Text:
"CXMT is not affiliated with the Chinese military,"

CXMT designs, produces, and sells its DRAM chips for civilian and commercial use, not for military use." The US Defense Department declined to comment on the specifics of the case. "As a matter of policy, the Department does not comment on pending or ongoing litigation,"

Why CXMT was placed on the Pentagon's list

"Since its initial designation in January 2025, CXMT has continuously suffered reputational and commercial harm,"

CXMT's role in the global chip market

Inside the lawsuit

"None of these determinations is supported by the factual record, by applicable law, or by reasoned decision-making,"

A pattern among Chinese companies

China's largest memory chipmaker, ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), has sued the Pentagon. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, the move comes after the company was placed on a list of companies the US government says support China's military. CXMT has also recently drawn attention after Apple reportedly made a special request to US officials regarding its status. The Cupertino-based tech giant has also reportedly held early talks with CXMT for iPhones and MacBooks which will be sold within the Chinese market. The lawsuit, filed this week, marks the latest escalation between Beijing's tech sector and Washington over trade restrictions tied to national security concerns.the company said in its federal lawsuit. "the agency told Reuters.The Pentagon first designated CXMT a Chinese military company under the Biden administration.The Trump administration kept the company on the list during a June update, despite CXMT's efforts to have the designation lifted.Even the list itself can have dire repercussions. Companies placed on it can be barred from doing business with the US government and suffer reputational damage that can affect business relationships even outside the government arena.CXMT said the designation has already cost it.the company said in a statement to Reuters, adding that the lawsuit is meant to protect its business interests going forward.CXMT is China's top producer of dynamic random-access memory chips, or DRAM, a type of memory chip used widely in smartphones, personal computers, servers, and artificial intelligence systems. The company's revenue jumped 874% in the first half of the year, according to the Reuters report, and it has expressed hopes of eventually entering the US market.CXMT filed its complaint in the US District Court for the District of Columbia. The lawsuit names the Department of Defense, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, and Assistant Secretary of Defense for Industrial Base Policy Michael Cadenazzi as defendants.The company said the Pentagon’s decision to designate it was “arbitrary,” not based on enough evidence, and violated its due-process rights. According to the complaint, CXMT provided information to the Pentagon for over a year to dispute the designation and get itself off the list.CXMT also pointed to a reversal earlier this year as evidence of inconsistent handling. The company said the Pentagon published a notice in February stating that CXMT would be removed from the list, then withdrew that notice the same day. CXMT alleges the Defense Department later relisted the company without adequately explaining the change.CXMT said in its complaint.CXMT's legal challenge follows a similar path taken by other major Chinese firms contesting their inclusion on the Pentagon's list. In June, Chinese technology and e-commerce giant Alibaba sued the US government over its own placement on the list.Precedent suggests such challenges can succeed. Smartphone and electric-vehicle maker Xiaomi filed a similar lawsuit in 2021 and was ultimately removed from the list.CXMT's case adds to a growing pattern of Chinese companies turning to US courts to contest national security-related designations, underscoring the tension between Washington's efforts to restrict China's access to advanced technology and Chinese firms' push to protect their standing in global markets, including their long-term ambitions in the US

Article Title: In 2017, US government introduced 60-day grace period for H-1B visa workers; 9 years later DHS wants to end it; here's the status update
Article Text:
The 6--day grace period for H1-B visa holders was introduced in 2017

What is the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers

What could happen if the grace period is removed

Why the move matters to Indian H-1B workers

What happens next

For nearly nine years, foreign workers in the US who lost their jobs have had a 60-day window to find a new employer or change their immigration status. Now, that protection may be removed. According to a Bloomberg Law report, a proposal from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to end the 60-day grace period has cleared a key White House review, moving it closer to becoming public. If approved, the proposal could have a major impact on H-1B visa holders, including thousands of Indian professionals, who are among the biggest users of the visa programme. However, the rule has not taken effect yet, and its final details are still not public.The grace period was introduced in 2017. It allows certain foreign workers and their dependents to remain in the US for up to 60 consecutive days after their employment ends, provided their authorised stay has not expired. During this period, workers can look for a new job, find another employer willing to sponsor them, or apply to change their immigration status.The rule covers several visa categories, including H-1B, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B1 and TN visa holders, along with eligible dependents.The provision has been particularly important for H-1B workers who face sudden layoffs, giving them limited time to make decisions without having to immediately leave the country.If the proposal is finalised as described, foreign workers whose jobs end before their authorised stay expires could face much tougher rules. They and their dependents could generally be required to leave the US immediately after losing their jobs. Changing employers or immigration status from within the country could also become more difficult unless US Citizenship and Immigration Services uses its discretion to forgive a lapse in status.The possible change comes at a time when job cuts and uncertainty in the technology sector have already raised concerns among skilled foreign workers.Indian nationals are among the biggest beneficiaries of the H-1B programme. They accounted for 71% of successful H-1B applicants in fiscal year 2024, according to the information provided.The proposal could therefore have a significant impact on Indian professionals and their families living in the US. The Indian-American population in the country is estimated at around 5.2 million.Former White House adviser Ajay Jain Bhutoria criticised the proposal and called for the grace period to be extended to 180 days instead."Eliminating the 60-day grace period is both inhumane and unworkable. When a high-skilled worker faces a sudden termination, 60 days is already dangerously short. Stripping away this protection entirely leaves thousands of law-abiding individuals with zero time to wrap up their lives,” said Bhutoria.He also said families could face serious disruption if workers are forced to leave immediately after losing their jobs.The next major step is the proposal's publication in the Federal Register. That will reveal exactly what DHS is proposing and start the public comment process before any final decision is made. For now, the key takeaway for H-1B workers is that the 60-day grace period remains in place. The White House review is an important step forward for the proposal, but it is not the final rule.The development is said to be part of a broader set of proposed policy changes affecting the H-1B programme, making the next steps closely watched by foreign workers, US employers and immigration experts alike.
Article Summary: 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders was introduced in 2017. It allows certain foreign workers and their dependents to remain in the US for up to 60 consecutive days after their employment ends, provided their authorised stay has not expired. During this period, workers can look for a new job, find another employer willing to sponsor them, or apply to change their immigration status.

Article Title: As JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon takes his annual bus trip with other executives; he says: It is very frustrating as the view is that America is very behind in ...
Article Text:
Jamie Dimon: ‘The notion that this country is behind is frustrating’

A $1.5 trillion bet on national security

Inside the tour

A cultural shift on the West Coast

What the security and resiliency initiative covers

Jamie Dimon, the CEO of America’s largest bank JPMorgan Chase has voiced his frustration over perceptions that America is falling behind in defense technology.“The notion that this country is behind is frustrating, but I’m very uplifted by what they’re doing,” Dimon told Axios while touring California defense startups including Impulse Space. Dimon’s comments come as JPMorgan Chase expands its Security and Resiliency Initiative, a $1.5 trillion program launched in October to support national security industries. Initially focused on the US, the effort now extends to Canada, Europe, and the U.K., with billions already committed across aerospace, defense, manufacturing, energy, and health tech.Riding a bus from Impulse Space toward an In-N-Out Burger somewhere southeast of Redondo Beach, California, Dimon and fellow JPMorgan executives spent the drive discussing the defense-tech sector's opportunities, risks, and blind spots. Dimon said it's frustrating to hear the narrative that the U.S. is falling behind, but that he personally feels uplifted by what companies like Impulse Space are actually building.The trip is tied to a much larger commitment. In October, JPMorgan Chase committed $1.5 trillion toward national security through its Security and Resiliency Initiative. What began as a domestic-focused push has since expanded to include Canada, Europe, and the U.K.,with billions of dollars already deployed and billions more potentially still to come.Dimon traced his own interest in the space back to Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which he said forced a broader rethink of weapons, tactics, and global power balances. He said conversations with retired generals about the resulting challenges were what really opened his eyes to the issue.Axios accompanied Dimon and his team on the trip, which included a visit to Impulse Space — a space-mobility startup led by SpaceX's first employee — along with meetings with missile, drone, and aircraft makers, energy specialists, manufacturers, and data companies.The visits were part of JPMorgan's annual bus tour tradition, in which Dimon and other senior bank executives travel to meet with employees, clients, and local communities across the country. This year's route was dedicated entirely to California, beginning in Healdsburg and moving through San Francisco, Modesto, Santa Barbara, and Los Angeles before wrapping up in Orange County.Defense work was once viewed with skepticism in parts of the West Coast tech world. That's changed. Startups and newer defense contractors clustered around LAX and SFO are now aggressively competing for Pentagon budget dollars and increasingly overshadowing older, more traditional defense contractors.John China, co-leader of JPMorgan Chase's innovation economy practice, said that in three decades in Silicon Valley, he's never seen a manufacturing push of this intensity, calling the current momentum real and tangible. JPMorgan sponsored this year's NatSec100, a ranking of prominent private-capital-backed defense companies and their government contracts; a dozen companies that previously appeared on the list have since gone public. China said the firm needs to keep showing up in person, regularly, to stay connected with the people building in this space.The initiative is focused on critical industries including aerospace and defense, manufacturing, energy, and health tech, spanning more than two dozen subcategories such as battery storage, command and control systems, critical minerals, munitions, shipbuilding, and space launch.The effort is backed by a notable roster of advisors, including former Defense Secretary Robert Gates, retired Generals Chris Cavoli and Paul Nakasone, and former House Speaker Paul Ryan. JPMorgan Chase co-president Doug Petno said the firm is putting both its people and its capital behind the effort, describing the commitment as one that needed to be substantive and backed by visible, measurable action rather than symbolic.The stakes, according to Dimon's teamThe broader argument driving the initiative is that if the U.S. fails to accelerate its defense-industrial base, fails to remove Chinese components from its most sensitive supply chains, and fails to balance competing priorities across the Asia-Pacific, the Middle East, and the Arctic, it risks losing the next major conflict
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon says the notion that the U.S. is falling behind in defense technology is 'frustrating' Dimon's comments come as the bank expands its Security and Resiliency Initiative, a $1.5 trillion program to support national security industries. The initiative is focused on aerospace and defense, manufacturing, energy, and health tech.

Article Title: Goldman Sachs exec does not 'agree' with banks using AI models of OpenAI, Anthropic and other, says: We are delegating what is very important to us
Article Text:

Reasoning is still important. You still need to reason about [problems] and structure it into an argument, and now we’re delegating reasoning,”

The threat to apprenticeship and Wall Street culture

The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across Wall Street risks undermining the analytical capabilities of future financial leaders, according to a senior Goldman Sachs executive directing one of the investment bank’s premier digital and AI initiatives. Speaking on a recent episode of the firm’s Exchanges podcast, Chris Churchman, a Goldman Sachs partner who heads the institutional client platform Marquee and co-chairs the bank’s Global Banking and Markets AI working group, cautioned that outsourcing fundamental problem-solving to automated models threatens core human reasoning.Churchman stated in remarks shared with CNBC.According to Churchman, just as everyday navigation and memorisation eroded with the modern navigational tools, financiers risk losing their core critical instincts if software performs all complex evaluations. This dynamic creates a double-edged sword for the financial sector: while deploying AI increases immediate profitability, it risks hollowing out the foundational skills junior staff need to develop into senior decision-makers.Churchman, who led foreign exchange trading at UBS prior to joining Goldman in 2021, highlighted that institutional expertise relies heavily on hands-on practice and unwritten, intuitive insights passed down across trading desks.While routines like handling client pricing requests can be entirely automated, bypassing those entry-level tasks raises concerns over whether future traders will fully grasp risk management. He also said that the reliance on AI also threatens entry-level headcount, following reports last year that Wall Street firms were exploring ways to use automation to reduce the proportion of junior analysts relative to senior staff.Next, for Churchman, systems must ensure staff members make the final judgment calls during high-stakes, ambiguous scenarios instead of acting as passive software monitors.Churchman also discussed the practical engineering realities of embedding AI into Marquee, Goldman’s proprietary platform used by hedge funds and institutional clients for trade execution, research, market data, and risk analytics.
Article Summary: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across Wall Street risks undermining the analytical capabilities of future financial leaders, according to a senior Goldman Sachs executive. Chris Churchman, a Goldman Sachs partner, cautioned that outsourcing fundamental problem-solving to automated models threatens core human reasoning. He also said that the reliance on AI also threatens entry-level headcount.

According to a 2017 HBO documentary, he would spend $2.61 on two sausage patties when the market was down, and splurge on a $3.17 bacon, egg, and cheese biscuit when it was up.Ikea's late founder, billionaire Ingvar Kamprad, shared a similar devotion to saving. The 31-year-old has embraced the FIRE (financially independent, retire early) movement, going as far as buying discounted clothing, skateboarding to work, and booking flights she later canceled just to eat for free in American Express airport lounges.Guo previously told Fortune.Taken together, these habits point to a pattern among some of the world's wealthiest people: financial success doesn't necessarily erase the instinct to hunt for a deal. For O'Leary, Buffett, Kamprad, and Guo, staying budget-conscious appears less about needing to save and more about a mindset that helped build their fortunes in the first place.
Article Summary: Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary has an estimated net worth of $400 million. The 72-year-old says he still heads straight to Walmart whenever he needs household essentials. Article Title: Why 1000 citizen scientists from 25 countries across the world buried their cotton underpants
Article Text:
Representative image

The more the underpants disappeared, the more active the soil was

Private gardens produced the biggest surprise

Why scientists chose underpants instead of expensive equipment

What happens when you bury a pair of cotton underpants in the ground and come back two months later? For nearly 1,000 citizen scientists in Switzerland, the answer offered an unusual window into the hidden world beneath their feet. In a large citizen science project, participants buried more than 2,000 pairs of cotton underpants and 12,000 tea bags at sites across Switzerland. The goal was not a prank. Researchers wanted to see whether the speed at which the cotton broke down could reveal how active the soil's living community was.The results, published on August 26 in New Phytologist Foundation, suggest that a simple pair of cotton underpants can provide useful clues about soil decomposition and fertility — while also helping people pay more attention to one of Earth's most important and often overlooked resources.Soil is filled with bacteria, fungi and other tiny organisms that break down organic matter. The researchers used cotton underpants as a simple way to observe this process.Participants buried two pairs at each site and dug them up after one and two months. The idea was simple: the more the cotton had decomposed, the more biologically active the soil was likely to be.After one month, the underpants had lost an average of about 10% of their material.After two months, average decomposition had reached more than 50%. The researchers called the measure the “Underpants Index” and compared it with the more established Tea Bag Index, which also measures how quickly organic material breaks down in soil.Where the underpants were buried made a major difference. Private gardens showed the highest average decomposition after two months, with around 58% of the material breaking down. Lawns showed the lowest rate at around 40%, while farmland and grasslands fell somewhere in between.Land use was the strongest factor affecting decomposition, the researchers found. Soil nutrients and other soil properties also played a role.The findings suggest that the underpants test may reflect soil fertility and biological decomposition activity more strongly than soil health in its broadest sense. That distinction matters because faster decomposition is not always a sign that a natural ecosystem is healthier.The unusual experiment had another purpose: making soil science easier for ordinary people to understand. Testing soil can require specialised equipment and technical knowledge. A buried pair of cotton underpants, however, offers a visual result that almost anyone can understand. Participants could simply see how much of the fabric had disappeared.The project also showed the power of citizen science. Around 1,000 people helped researchers collect data from hundreds of locations — a scale that would have been difficult for a small research team to achieve alone.The researchers say the method is not a complete test of soil health. But it can offer a simple first look at what is happening below the surface and help people understand that soil is far more than just dirt.After all, for this experiment, the condition of a pair of buried underpants helped tell a much bigger story about the living world beneath our feet.
Article Summary: Citizen scientists in Switzerland buried 2,000 pairs of cotton underpants and 12,000 tea bags at sites across Switzerland. After one month, the underpants had lost an average of about 10% of their material. After two months, average decomposition had reached more than 50%.

Article Title: Researchers faced more than 100 million possible ways to 3D-print a NASA rocket alloy; AI picked just 40 experiments and found 6 that worked, including the first successful print at only 500 watts
Article Text:
Representative Image

"Ninety per cent of commercial printers cannot print this metal alloy, so given that we were able to find these feasible process parameters, it allows us to use those commercial printers, and we are essentially democratising the printing of this alloy,"

A NASA alloy built for extreme heat

"Sometimes they printed a certain configuration, and the product just melted,"

"It wasn't really printable, and even with time and money, they wouldn't be able to try all 100 million options.

What we were doing in our collaboration is to apply the AI so that we efficiently choose candidates from this very large search space."

AI searches more than 100 million possibilities

"They would give me back the results, and I liked all of them - even if they failed -- because every result improved our AI model,"

Lower power could expand access

"It's a very challenging case for AI,"

"Every time you try, you basically get a binary success or failure signal, and you are trying to minimise the number of tries that you have so that you get to those successful needles very quickly."

A broader tool for scientific discovery

"There's always uncertainty when you are deploying something where real people, materials, and physical costs are involved,"

"We didn't know whether we would succeed or not, and there is always that risk. There are real stakes. I was very surprised that we were able to do this so well."

Washington State University researchers used artificial intelligence (AI) to identify a faster, less costly way to 3D print a high-performance metal alloy. This has avoided the need to manually test more than 100 million possible printing configurations.The advance could eventually make the alloy, widely used in aerospace applications and potentially useful in other industries, printable on more common commercial equipment. The AI strategy developed by the team could also help with other scientific problems involving enormous numbers of possible experiments, including drug discovery.Researchers from WSU's School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and the School of Mechanical and Materials Engineering published the work in the Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. The project also received the Innovative Deployed Application Award at the organization's annual conference.said Jana Doppa, Huie-Rogers Endowed Chair Professor of Computer Science and Berry Distinguished Professor in Engineering, who led the research, WSU Insider reported.GRCop-42 is an alloy of copper, chromium and niobium. NASA designed it for extreme environments where it must withstand heat while also transferring it. This alloy is employed in aerospace systems such as combustion chambers of liquid rocket engines because of its high thermal conductivity and strength at very high temperatures.However, the alloy is hard and expensive to 3D print, despite its good properties and wider potential, because the process typically requires a lot of laser power and energy.The technique, called Directed Energy Deposition, could also help coat existing jet engine alloys with GRCop-42, researchers noted, since raising engine operating temperatures by 50 degrees Celsius can improve fuel efficiency by up to 10 per cent.Previous attempts to print GRCop-42 using the lower wattages available on more common commercial machines had not succeeded. Testing possible printing settings one by one is also impractical. Each attempt consumes expensive material, requires specialised equipment, and takes considerable human effort. A single print can cost hundreds of dollars, and thoroughly analysing the finished sample can require several days.said Azza Fadhel, first author of the paper and a PhD student in computer science.The researchers started with data from 37 printing configurations that had already failed in earlier experiments conducted in the School of Mechanical and Materials Engineering.Using those results, they developed a method that could estimate how likely an untested combination of settings was to produce a successful print. The AI model then recommended small groups of new configurations to test.Its selections balanced two priorities. Some experiments focused on configurations that appeared especially promising, while others explored less certain parts of the search space that could provide new information and improve the model.Nathaniel Zuckschwerdt, Susmita Bose, and Amit Bandyopadhyay in the School of Mechanical and Materials Engineering worked with the team to print GRCop-42 using the configurations chosen by the AI and then evaluate the finished samples. Aryan Deshwal from the University of Minnesota also collaborated on the project.said Fadhel.Successfully printing the alloy with less laser power could bring several advantages. It could reduce energy consumption, decrease wear on printing equipment, and lower the costs associated with processing samples after printing.It could also make GRCop-42 available to universities, smaller laboratories, and companies without access to specialised high-power printing systems.The difficulty was that researchers already knew successful settings would be extremely rare among the more than 100 million possible configurations.said Doppa.Despite those odds, the team found six successful configurations at different laser power levels over three months of work, while limiting the project to just 40 experiments. For the first time, they successfully printed GRCop-42 using 500 watts of laser power.The researchers say the same AI-guided approach could be adapted to identify workable processing conditions for other metal alloys and additive manufacturing systems.More broadly, the method could help scientists tackle problems in which successful results are uncommon, the number of possible experiments is enormous, and testing every option would be prohibitively expensive. The researchers see potential applications beyond manufacturing, including other areas of scientific discovery where each experiment carries significant material, financial, or time costs.said Doppa.
Article Summary: Washington State University researchers used artificial intelligence (AI) to identify a faster, less costly way to 3D print a high-performance metal alloy. This has avoided the need to manually test more than 100 million possible printing configurations. The advance could eventually make the alloy, widely used in aerospace applications, printable on more common commercial equipment.

The tech giant has announced two new app quality requirements on Google Play, one focused on cutting apps' memory usage, and another aimed at securing device migrations, with clear consequences for developers who don't comply.In a blog post, Raghavendra Hareesh Pottamsetty, GM of Google Play Developer & Monetization wrote,To address this, Android is rolling out broader memory limits designed to stop individual apps from hogging device memory and slowing down the entire system.Google Play is now setting performance thresholds across three areas: dynamic memory usage (an app's private data storage), bitmap memory usage, and code optimisation. Apps published on Google Play will need at least 25% coverage across optimisation, shrinking, and obfuscation using tools like R8. The message to developers is blunt: exceed these limits, andTo help developers prepare, Google has started rolling out new diagnostic tools in Play Console, including deeper memory metrics in Android vitals, a filter to trackcrashes, DEX code optimisation insights for every uploaded app bundle, and proactive alerts when apps exceed the new thresholds.More tools, including deeper insights into the Android Memory Limiter feature, are expected later this year.Enforcement begins in February 2027. Apps and games that fail to meet the thresholds may seethough Google says it will share additional details later this year.Alongside the memory rules, Google is introducing a Zero-Tap Sign-In standard, requiring apps that support user sign-in to automatically restore a user's sign-in state when they switch to a new Android device, using the Android Restore Credentials API. Starting in April 2027, apps will need to meet this requirement to maintain full publishing capabilities and visibility in the Play Store. Games are currently exempt, though Google says tailored guidance for gaming authentication is coming in 2027.The timing isn't a coincidence. The memory limits were first introduced with Android 17 on Pixel phones, and the base configurations of the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL reportedly ship with less RAM than last year's models. As Android 17 spreads across the wider ecosystem, Google is warning developers to prepare for a much broader range of device memory configurations, from 4GB to 16GB and beyond.
Article Summary: Google announces two new requirements for Android apps. One focuses on cutting apps' memory usage, the other on securing sign-ins during device migrations. Android is rolling out broader memory limits designed to stop individual apps from hogging device memory and slowing down the entire system.
